name: Cherokee
variety: Oklahoma (Western) Cherokee, as recorded in Feeling's Cherokee-English Dictionary (1975) and described by Montgomery-Anderson (2008) and Uchihara (2016); North Carolina Cherokee has a simpler tone system and keeps the glottal stop where Oklahoma has the lowfall tone
sources: Feeling, Durbin (1975). Cherokee-English Dictionary, edited by William Pulte. Tahlequah: Cherokee Nation of Oklahoma.
Pulte, William & Feeling, Durbin (1975). Outline of Cherokee grammar. In Feeling (1975).
Montgomery-Anderson, Brad (2008). A Reference Grammar of Oklahoma Cherokee. PhD dissertation, University of Kansas.
Uchihara, Hiroto (2016). Tone and Accent in Oklahoma Cherokee. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Herrick, Dylan, Berardo, Marcellino, Feeling, Durbin, Hirata-Edds, Tracy & Peter, Lizette (2015). Collaborative documentation and revitalization of Cherokee tone. Language Documentation & Conservation 9, 12-31.

Lindsey, Geoffrey (1985). Intonation and Interrogation: Tonal Structure and the Expression of a Pragmatic Function in English and Other Languages. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles.
Wright, Richard (1996). Tone and accent in Oklahoma Cherokee. In Pamela Munro (ed.), Cherokee Papers from UCLA. Los Angeles: UCLA Department of Linguistics.
Johnson, Keith (2005). Tone and pitch accent in Cherokee nouns. Manuscript, University of California, Berkeley.
Uchihara, Hiroto (2009). High tone in Oklahoma Cherokee. International Journal of American Linguistics 75, 317-336.
Scancarelli, Janine (2005). Cherokee. In Heather K. Hardy & Janine Scancarelli (eds.), Native Languages of the Southeastern United States. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press.
Cook, William H. (1979). A Grammar of North Carolina Cherokee. PhD dissertation, Yale University.
contrasts: six pitch patterns on the syllable: low, high, rising, falling, lowfall and superhigh
short versus long vowels in six qualities; the sixth vowel, written v, is a nasalised central vowel
unaspirated versus aspirated stops and affricates (written d, g, gw, j, dl versus t, k, kw, ch, tl in the usual romanisation)
glottal stop and h as consonants, also before and after other consonants
no labial stops or labial fricatives; m occurs in few native words
allophony: unaspirated stops and affricates range from voiceless unaspirated to voiced, and are voiced above all between vowels (hence the spellings d, g, gw, j, dl); aspirated ones arise from a stop followed by h
/ts/ is palatal [tʃ ~ dʒ] in Oklahoma; aspirated /tɬʰ/ is usually the lateral fricative [ɬ] (written hl)
sonorants next to h are voiceless (hn, hl, hw, hy)
a short vowel before h is devoiced
vowels are nasalised after a nasal consonant and at the end of a word
word-final vowels are short and nasalised and carry a predictable high-falling pitch; in connected speech they are pronounced only before a pause and otherwise dropped
/a/ is a low central vowel; /ə̃/ is mid central and always nasal
where Oklahoma Cherokee has a lowfall tone, North Carolina Cherokee keeps a glottal stop (Lindsey 1985)
syllable_structure: (C)V(ː) as written in the syllabary; in speech h, ʔ and s add to the consonant before or after the vowel, and vowel loss creates further clusters
phonotactics: words of the citation form end in a vowel
h and ʔ combine freely with other consonants; s may precede a stop
contour tones, lowfall and superhigh occur on long vowels, level tones on short and long vowels, with few exceptions
the syllabary writes neither vowel length, tone, aspiration in all cases, nor the glottal stop

stress.rule: There is no lexical stress. The superhigh tone behaves as an accent: a word has at most one, on its rightmost long vowel, and it is assigned by the morphology and syntax (Uchihara 2016).

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: short vowels are devoiced before h and final vowels are dropped in connected speech; vowel quality is not reduced
rhythm.notes: No rhythm study is known to me; the class is a neutral default. The tone-bearing unit is the mora and long vowels are about twice as long as short ones, which points to timing by morae. Final vowels are short, so final lengthening is set to weak.

length.notes: A long vowel takes about twice as long as a short one (Montgomery-Anderson 2008). Neither the syllabary nor the plain romanisation writes length.

intonation.declarative: the lexical tones are kept; the last vowel before a pause carries a high fall
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the clitics =s, =sgo or =ju on the first word; melody not described in the sources consulted
intonation.wh_question: question word first; melody not described in the sources consulted
intonation.continuation: not described in the sources consulted
intonation.accent_shape: the superhigh tone: a rise from high to the top of the range on a long vowel
intonation.notes: The averaged tone contours of one male speaker span 88 to 127 Hz, single tokens 81 to 141 Hz (Herrick et al. 2015); Johnson (2005) found about 80 to 140 Hz for two male speakers, final fall included.

inventory.name: low (called mid by Pulte & Feeling; tone 2)
inventory.description: level low, the default tone, on short and long vowels; measured 104 falling slightly to 96 Hz

inventory.name: high (tone 3)
inventory.description: level high, on short and long vowels; measured 108 rising slightly to 112 Hz

inventory.name: rising (low-high, tone 23)
inventory.description: rise from low to high on a long vowel; measured 97 to 109 Hz

inventory.name: falling (high-low, tone 32)
inventory.description: fall from high to low on a long vowel; measured 122 to 97 Hz, starting above the level high tone

inventory.name: lowfall (tone 1, also written 21)
inventory.description: fall from low to the bottom of the range on a long vowel; measured 106 to 88 Hz; goes back to a glottal stop after the vowel

inventory.name: superhigh (tone 4, also written 34; highfall in Montgomery-Anderson)
inventory.description: rise from high to the top of the range on a long vowel; measured 109 to 127 Hz; acts as the accent of the word

inventory.name: final high fall (boundary tone, 43)
inventory.description: predictable high-falling pitch on the short nasalised vowel at the end of a word before a pause; not a lexical tone

sandhi: a high tone spreads onto neighbouring morae, in both directions under different conditions (Uchihara 2016)
the lowfall tone arises where a glottal stop after a long vowel was lost
the superhigh accent falls on the rightmost long vowel and marks certain grammatical forms, such as adjectives, nouns derived from verbs and subordinate verbs
tone.neutral_tone: morae without a tone of their own are low
tone.notes: The Chao digits are the four-level numerals of Pulte & Feeling (1975), in which 1 is the lowest level and 4 the highest; they are not a five-level measurement. The measured values are the first and last of five points averaged over the vowels of one male speaker over 65 (Herrick et al. 2015, 156 vowels). The literature counts five to seven surface tones; six is the usual number.

phonation: voiceless sonorants and devoiced short vowels next to h
nasalised vowels after nasals and at the end of a word
glottal stop; the lowfall tone continues an earlier glottal stop

problems: the Cherokee syllabary is not supported: the rules cover only romanised text in the style of the Cherokee-English Dictionary, and syllabary text is read as unknown letters

tone is spoken only if it is written with the superscript digits of the dictionary (¹ ² ³ ⁴ and their combinations); ordinary romanised text, which has no tone marks, gets no lexical tone at all, only the high fall on the last vowel
vowel length depends on the underdot of the dictionary for short vowels; in text without it every non-final vowel is long
long vowels are three times as long as short ones (300 against 100 units), against a ratio of about two in the literature
the vowel a uses the rounded back vowel of English 'lot' ([ɒ]) instead of a low central [a]
g is voiced but has the burst of an aspirated k added to it, which blurs the contrast between plain g and aspirated k
tl, dl and hl are sequences with a voiced l; there is no lateral affricate or fricative
short vowels before h are not devoiced (noted as an open problem in the phoneme file)
good: all six tones of the literature have tone phonemes (1, 2, 23, 32, 3, 4), with contours taken from the measurements of Herrick et al. (2015), plus the final high fall (43)
final vowels are short and nasalised; vowels after nasals are nasalised
no word stress: every syllable has the same stress level, length and amplitude
the vowel v is a nasalised central vowel

notes: Pitch values are for one older male speaker; a synthesiser should scale them to the pitch range of the voice. Montgomery-Anderson (2008) analyses the six patterns as combinations of low, high and falling morae.
